transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see us today?

My mind is constantly racing about the practice and the future, and I just can’t shut the worrying off anymore. It has gotten to the point where I feel like I can't relax, even when I'm away from the office, and my wife and colleagues urged me to seek some help.
Have you experienced any recurring, distressing memories or thoughts related to a specific traumatic event, or are your worries more about everyday things like work or the future?

No, I haven't experienced any past trauma or distressing memories like that. My worries are entirely focused on everyday concerns about my dental practice, my employees' security, and transitioning into retirement. These thoughts just constantly loop in my mind and I can't seem to stop them.
Do you experience any physical symptoms like palpitations, sweating, or trembling when these worries peak, or are they mainly just mental concerns?

No, I don't really experience physical symptoms like palpitations, sweating, or trembling when I worry. It is mainly a mental struggle with my mind constantly racing, though I do end up feeling incredibly tired and physically drained from all the stress.
Have you noticed any changes in your interest or pleasure in activities you normally enjoy, such as hobbies or spending time with family and friends, since your worrying started?

Yes, I've definitely lost enjoyment in my usual activities. I've cut back on hiking and painting because even setting up my art supplies feels like too much effort, and I've been turning down social invitations because I feel so drained. My wife has also noticed that I'm barely present at home anymore, even when we're sitting in the same room.
Do you feel sad or empty most of the day, or is it more that you're anxious and worried, but not necessarily feeling sad?

It is definitely much more about the intense anxiety and constant worry rather than feeling sad or empty. My brain just feels stuck in high gear, constantly looping through "what-if" scenarios about the practice and my retirement, rather than feeling depressed.
Can you estimate how long you've been experiencing this intense worry and loss of enjoyment in activities, and has it been a constant state or have you had periods where you felt better in between?

This has been going on pretty steadily for about a year and a quarter, ever since I really started trying to line up my retirement and the buy-in with the younger dentists. It has been a constant, steady state of worry, and I haven't really had any periods where I felt better or got a break from it.

You mentioned losing enjoyment in activities like hiking and painting, but can you tell me if there are any activities or situations where you still feel some pleasure or interest, even if it's fleeting?

To be honest, it is currently very difficult to find enjoyment or interest in anything at all. Even when I attempt to do something else, the constant worry and racing thoughts about the practice block out any fleeting sense of pleasure. It just leaves me feeling completely drained instead.
Are there any small, everyday things that still bring you some sense of pleasure or satisfaction, even if it's minor, like a good cup of coffee or a beautiful sunset?

To be honest, even those small moments don't bring much satisfaction anymore. Things like having a cup of coffee or walking the dog just feel like a chore because my mind is constantly running numbers about the practice. I'm just too drained to appreciate them.

You've mentioned feeling anxious and worried, but not necessarily sad or empty, can you tell me if you've had any days in the past two weeks where you didn't feel anxious or worried at all, or has it been a constant presence?

No, there hasn't been a single day in the past two weeks where I haven't felt anxious. My mind feels constantly stuck in high gear, looping through thoughts about the practice day and night, and I haven't had a single day where I felt truly relaxed or free from this worry.

You've described feeling anxious and worried, but also mentioned losing interest in activities and feeling drained; can you tell me if you've had any thoughts about death or wishing you weren't alive, or are your thoughts more focused on the worries about your practice and future?

No, I definitely don't have any thoughts of death or wishing I wasn't alive. My mind is just entirely consumed by the constant, looping worries about the practice, my employees' security, the associates' buy-in, and my retirement future. I just want to find a way to quiet my mind.
Are there any activities or things that you used to enjoy that you still find yourself looking forward to, even if you don't end up feeling pleasure from them when you do them?

I still think about wanting to paint, go hiking, or socialize, and I really wish I could. But when it comes to actually setting up my painting gear or getting out on a trail, the sheer effort of starting feels completely overwhelming. I'm just too exhausted and mentally preoccupied to actually do them or find any enjoyment.

You've mentioned feeling anxious and worried, but also losing interest in activities; can you tell me if you think your lack of interest in activities is more due to your anxiety and worry, or if you feel like you're just not interested in things anymore, even if your anxiety were to decrease?

It is definitely because of the anxiety and worry. My mind is so constantly consumed by the practice and I feel too physically and mentally drained to even try. If I could just stop this constant worrying and get my energy back, I would gladly return to painting and hiking.

If your anxiety and worries about the practice were to significantly decrease, do you think you would regain your interest and pleasure in activities like painting and hiking, or do you think you would still struggle with feeling empty or disconnected from things you used to enjoy?

I absolutely believe I would regain my interest once this constant worry and mental exhaustion are resolved. I didn't stop because I lost my love for painting and hiking, but because my mind is constantly looping over the practice and I feel too physically and mentally drained to even set up my easel or go for a walk.

If you were able to completely resolve your worries about the practice and your retirement, do you think you would still feel a lack of interest or pleasure in activities, or would that improve as well?

I believe it would definitely improve. My lack of interest in painting or hiking is entirely tied to this constant worrying and physical exhaustion. If my mind could finally quiet down, I'm confident I would have the energy and mental presence to enjoy those activities again.

You've mentioned that your main issue is anxiety and worry, but you've also experienced a loss of interest in activities; can you tell me if you think you would still feel anxious and worried if you were able to regain your interest and pleasure in activities like painting and hiking?

Yes, I would definitely still feel anxious, because the worry is the root cause preventing me from enjoying those hobbies in the first place. Even if I forced myself to go hiking or paint, my mind would just keep looping and branching off with thoughts about the practice, making it impossible to distract myself. The anxiety would remain because I simply cannot shut off these racing thoughts, even during activities I used to love.
You've described both anxiety and a loss of interest in activities, but can you tell me if you've experienced any significant changes in your appetite or sleep patterns since your worrying started?

My appetite hasn't really changed, but my sleep has been absolutely terrible. Most nights I lie awake for an hour or two running numbers about the practice in my head, and even when I do fall asleep, I wake up at three or four in the morning worrying about payroll or the associates and just can't drift back off.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks where you felt consistently sad, empty, or depressed, separate from your current anxiety and worry about the practice?

No, I've never really experienced periods of feeling consistently sad, empty, or depressed like that. My struggle has always been this constant, overwhelming worry and anxiety about the practice rather than feeling down.
Can you describe a typical day and how your anxiety and worry affect your daily functioning and relationships, and are there any times when your worry seems to peak or worsen?

During the day, it's causing me to make small charting mistakes at the office and lose concentration during procedures, while at home, my wife says I'm barely present and I've been turning down social plans because I'm so drained. The worry definitely peaks at night, where I'll lie awake for hours running numbers or wake up at 3:00 AM unable to get back to sleep. It's incredibly frustrating because I just can't seem to turn it off.
Do you think your lack of interest in activities is a direct result of your anxiety and worry, or do you feel like you've lost interest in things independently of your anxiety?

It is absolutely a direct result of my anxiety and worry. I haven't lost interest in hiking, painting, or socializing on my own, but my mind is constantly spinning with worries about the practice, leaving me too keyed up and drained to participate. The constant worrying just leaves me with absolutely no mental or physical energy to engage in or enjoy those things.

If you were to wake up tomorrow and all your worries about the practice were suddenly and completely resolved, do you think you would still feel a general sense of sadness or emptiness, or would you primarily feel relieved and able to enjoy activities again?

I would feel an immense sense of relief, as I don't have any deep, independent sadness or emptiness inside me. It's just this non-stop loop of anxiety about the practice that is completely exhausting me, and if that were gone, I know I'd finally have the energy to relax at home and enjoy painting and hiking again.
Can you tell me if there are any times when you feel like you're worrying about your worry itself, or if your worry is always focused on specific issues like the practice and retirement?

No, I don't really worry about the worry itself; my thoughts are always focused on those concrete issues like the future of my practice, the associates' buy-in, and my staff's security. While I'm incredibly frustrated and exhausted by my inability to shut my mind off, my brain just constantly loops back to those real-world concerns. It's the actual future of the office and my retirement that keeps me up, not the fact that I am worrying.

Can you tell me if you've ever felt like you're at a point where you're worried that you might be worried too much, or is your worry always about something specific like the practice, and never about the worry process itself?

While my worries are focused on specific things like the practice, my staff, and retirement, I am deeply distressed by the worry process itself. It is incredibly frustrating that my brain feels constantly stuck in high gear and the thoughts loop uncontrollably. No matter how hard I try, I just cannot turn the worrying off, and that feeling of having no control over my own mind is exhausting.

You've described a constant state of worry and anxiety, but also a loss of interest in activities; can you tell me if you think your anxiety is the primary issue, and the loss of interest is a result of that, or if you think you might be experiencing some depressive symptoms as well?

The constant anxiety and mental racing are definitely the primary issue here, rather than a standalone depression. My loss of interest in painting, hiking, and socializing stems directly from being completely drained by the constant worry—it honestly feels like someone pulled the plug on my batteries. I'm just too mentally exhausted and unable to turn my mind off to engage in anything else.
If your anxiety about the practice and retirement were to completely disappear, do you think you would still feel a lack of interest or pleasure in activities, or would that improve as well?

I am certain that my interest and pleasure in those activities would completely return once the anxiety is gone. The only thing holding me back right now is that the constant worrying leaves me completely drained and preoccupied. If my mind could finally quiet down, I know I would have the energy and focus to enjoy painting, hiking, and socializing again.
Do you think that if your anxiety were treated and significantly improved, you would still experience a lack of interest in activities, or would that also improve with your anxiety?

Yes, it would absolutely improve along with the anxiety, because my lack of interest in painting and hiking is directly caused by being constantly exhausted, keyed up, and consumed by worry. I am very optimistic that if the racing thoughts were treated, I would regain my energy and gladly return to those hobbies. Right now, I'm just too drained by the constant worry to even try.
If you were able to completely resolve your worries about the practice, do you think you would still feel a lack of interest or pleasure in activities, or would that improve as well?

I am confident it would improve, as my lack of interest in painting, hiking, and socializing is directly tied to this constant worrying and exhaustion. I only stopped those activities because my mind is too consumed by the practice and I feel too physically drained to even try. If those worries were resolved, I believe my energy and enjoyment for my hobbies would return.

If you were to wake up tomorrow feeling completely relaxed and worry-free about the practice, do you think you would still feel a general sense of sadness or emptiness, or would you feel more like your old self, enjoying activities and feeling motivated?

I would definitely feel like my old self again, as I don't have any deep, independent sadness or emptiness. My lack of motivation and stepping away from painting, hiking, and socializing is purely because the constant, looping worry and terrible sleep leave me completely drained of energy. If that heavy mental burden about the practice were lifted, I would gladly and eagerly return to the activities I've always loved.

If you were to wake up tomorrow and all your worries about the practice were suddenly and completely resolved, do you think you would still feel a lack of interest or pleasure in activities, or would you primarily feel relieved and able to enjoy activities again, and would that relief last or would you eventually return to feeling anxious or worried about something else?

It’s honestly hard to imagine that scenario because the worries about the practice feel so consuming right now. I'm really not sure whether I would truly feel relieved and get back to my hobbies, or if my mind would just find something else to worry about.

Can you tell me if there are any times when you feel hopeless about your situation or like you're a burden to others, or are your thoughts primarily focused on the worries about your practice and future?

No, I don't feel hopeless or like a burden to others. My thoughts are almost entirely consumed by constant worries, "what-if" scenarios, and the logistics regarding my practice, my staff, and retirement. My mind is simply stuck in overdrive, looping and second-guessing my decisions about the future.

If you were to feel completely better from your anxiety, do you think you would still experience any symptoms of depression, such as feeling sad, empty, or disconnected from things, or would all your symptoms improve?

I'm not entirely sure, because I don't really feel depressed or empty, just incredibly anxious and exhausted from the constant worry. I suspect that if the anxiety finally went away, I would probably feel back to my normal self.
